correctness.rationale: A point is missed by the three closed translates exactly when the three relevant characters are all -1. The sum of the product of their three factors (1-chi) expands to 22-T, using the three vanishing single sums and the three pair sums of -1. Each missed point contributes 8; each center with both differences nonsquare contributes 4. Thus 22-T=8M+4R. Hasse bounds |T| by 10, so coverage is equivalent to R=3 and T=10. Normalizing the triple gives T=chi(t)T_lambda, and R=3 forces t nonsquare. The independently recovered cubic-sum table has T_lambda=-10 only at 13 and 18, the two roots of lambda^2-lambda+1; both lambda and lambda-1 are squares there. A direct independent test of all 2,300 subsets found exactly the asserted 100 covers, all 600 ordered parametrizations mapping six-to-one onto those covers, and the same orbit of the given representative under the 300 affine-square maps. Inversion swaps the two roots, so swapping the second and third points converts one root to the other without changing the nonsquare condition on t. The stabilizer order follows, and the pair intersection sizes 6 and 7 exclude any two-center cover.
residual_risks: The check concerns the specified field and the affine-square group, not general fields or the full Paley automorphism group.

evidence: Auer–Top section 3 recalls the exact supersingular-parameter criterion: roots of the Deuring polynomial with squared binomial coefficients. Proposition 2.2, invoked in the proof of their proposition 3.1, gives the group (Z/(p'-1)Z)^2, where p'=(-1)^((p-1)/2)p, for the supersingular Legendre curve over F_(p^2). At p=5 this gives 16 points. Zhou–Wu give general covering bounds, not the decisive coverage here.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Specialization to p=5 gives exactly the polynomial lambda^2-lambda+1 and character sum 16-26=-10. Conversely the required trace is divisible by p, hence the curve is supersingular. Thus the general theorem gives the exact normalized parameters of the extremal Paley triples in this field.

evidence: Normalize a triangle at a square difference to (0,1,lambda); its character sum remains -10. The Auer–Top Legendre theorem supplies exactly the reciprocal roots, with both lambda and 1-lambda square for supersingular parameters, using the symmetry lambda -> 1-lambda. Here -1 is square. Nonsquare scaling converts the zero-common-neighbor triangles to the covering triples.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: There are 25 translations, 12 nonsquare differences, and two reciprocal ratios; each unordered triple has six orderings. Hence 100. Swapping the second and third points inverts the ratio and changes the difference by a square multiplier, so all covers are affine-square equivalents; the stabilizer is 300/100. These are direct consequences of the older exact criterion with elementary normalization and orbit arithmetic, not a new classification gap closed by the census.

evidence: A+Q=F means the three vertices dominate the Paley graph using closed neighborhoods. The uncovered points are exactly the common neighbors of the three vertices in the complement. Nonsquare multiplication identifies the complement with the Paley graph, changing independent triples into triangles. Brouwer–Martin's expansion and Hasse bound imply that a triangle with no common neighbor at q=25 has S=-10, and that no other type of triple can have zero common neighbors.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: For zero common neighbors, their q-3+S=8[111]+4R gives 22+S=4R with S >= -10 and R <= 3, forcing S=-10 and R=3. Both directions of this equivalence follow from the same identity. Thus the cover problem is exactly the already studied endpoint over q=25, up to the nonsquare dilation. The later shattering result uses the square-difference family, not identical covers, even though nonsquare scaling exchanges the two geometric families.

originality.rationale: The classification is correct but is a direct specialization of two earlier results. Brouwer–Martin's proposition 0.1 proof applied in the complementary Paley graph forces a zero common-neighbor triple at q=25 to attain the elliptic Hasse endpoint, with R=3. Their proposition 0.3 proof explicitly relates the endpoints to supersingular Legendre parameters and nonsquare dilation. Auer–Top give both the Deuring polynomial criterion and the point count of the supersingular Legendre curves over the prime-square field. At p=5 the polynomial is exactly 1+4 lambda+lambda^2, and the supersingular Legendre point count is 16, i.e. T_lambda=-10. Conversely 16 points give trace 10 divisible by 5, hence supersingularity, as also used for the endpoint in Brouwer–Martin. Thus the two parameters are forced without a new enumeration, the nonsquare twist changes the trace sign, and the count and single orbit follow from ordered triples and the reciprocal pair of roots. This is a mathematical coverage finding, not an inference from an uncited later remark or a bare matching parameter.
residual_risks: An earlier source might state the count verbatim; that is not needed for the verified direct implication. The later catalogue's unnamed attribution does not settle bibliographic priority.
